cards.explanation: The answer is a blustering wind. Bildad does not hold back. He asks Job how long he will go on saying such things, then says, "The words of your mouth are a blustering wind." (Job 8:2) That is Bildad calling Job's whole speech a gust of wind. I think that is a rough way to open, friends.

The answer is that He gave them over to their rebellion. Bildad says, "When your children sinned against Him, He gave them over to their rebellion." (Job 8:4) That is what Bildad says about Job's children, and it is a hard thing to say to their father. I think this one hurts. Notice that these are Bildad's words, and he is the one making the claim.

The answer is mercy. Bildad says, "But if you would earnestly seek God and ask the Almighty for mercy…" (Job 8:5) Mercy is what he tells Job to ask for. This is the first of his ifs, and the ifs keep coming, friends. Hold on to this one, because the next verse stacks another on top.

The word is restore. Bildad says that if Job is pure and upright, "…even now He will rouse Himself on your behalf and restore your righteous estate." (Job 8:6) Restore means to put back what was there before. Bildad ties it to an if, and that is worth noticing, bakers.

The answer is False. Bildad says, "Though your beginnings were modest, your latter days will flourish." (Job 8:7) The beginnings are modest and the latter days are the big ones. He is painting a bright picture for Job, friends, with his ifs attached.

The answer is that they were born yesterday and know nothing. Bildad says, "For we were born yesterday and know nothing; our days on earth are but a shadow." (Job 8:9) He puts himself in with Job when he says "we." It's an odd thing to admit right after a lecture. Still, it's why he points Job to the generations before them.

The answer is True. Bildad asks, "Will they not teach you and tell you, and speak from their understanding?" (Job 8:10) He is sure the past generations have something to teach Job. He asks it as a question, but I think he already knows the answer he wants.

The answer is that they dry up faster than grass. Bildad says, "While the shoots are still uncut, they dry up more quickly than grass." (Job 8:12) Even uncut, they dry up fast. That is the picture he paints, friends. Grass isn't known for sticking around, so beating it is quite the race.
The word is forget. Bildad says, "Such is the destiny of all who forget God; so the hope of the godless will perish." (Job 8:13) The papyrus and reeds are his picture for that, bakers.

The answer is in a spider's web. Bildad says, "His confidence is fragile; his security is in a spider’s web." (Job 8:14) That is not much to put your weight on, friends. A spider's web is made to catch bugs, not to hold a person up.

The answer is False. Bildad says that if the plant is uprooted, its place "…will disown him, saying, ‘I never saw you.’" (Job 8:18) I think that is a cold goodbye. The place acts as if it never saw the plant.

The answer is True. Bildad says, "Surely this is the joy of his way; yet others will spring from the dust." (Job 8:19) So others will spring from the dust, friends. That's what the verse says, and I'll leave the rest alone.

The word is reject. Bildad says, "Behold, God does not reject the blameless, nor will He strengthen the hand of evildoers." (Job 8:20) It's his big finish, bakers, and he sets the blameless and the evildoers side by side.

The answer is laughter. Bildad says, "He will yet fill your mouth with laughter, and your lips with a shout of joy." (Job 8:21) That's a warm line from a speech that started cold. Laughter is my kind of promise, friends, and I'm glad it's in the passage.

The answer is False. Bildad says, "Your enemies will be clothed in shame, and the tent of the wicked will be no more." (Job 8:22) So it's shame, not honor. That's how he ends his whole speech, friends.
